title: Why Am I Not Showing Up on Google Maps? (Contractor Fix List)
h1: Why Am I Not Showing Up on Google Maps?
meta: Not showing up on Google Maps? The usual causes for contractors: an incomplete profile, too few reviews, a wrong service area, or a suspended listing. Here's the fix list, in order.
short: If you're invisible in the map pack, it's almost never bad luck. It's one of five fixable things: an incomplete profile, not enough reviews, the wrong service area, a name/address/phone mismatch, or a suspension you were never told about. Work the list in order.
statLabel: Median reviews for an HVAC shop in the map pack — the bar you're being measured against

body.answer: An incomplete profile can't outrank a complete one.
body.html: Google ranks what it can verify. Every empty field — services, hours, service area, description, categories, photos — is a reason to rank someone else. Fill all of it, pick the most specific primary category you legitimately fit, and add job photos weekly. This is free, and it's the single highest-return hour in contractor marketing. Full list: the Google Business Profile checklist.

body.h2: 2. You don't have enough reviews yet
body.answer: Review count is the bar — and it's higher than most shops think.
body.html: The shops sitting in the map pack aren't there on charm. The median HVAC shop ranking locally carries about 519 reviews; for plumbers it's about 337. If you have 20, you're not competing yet — you're warming up. And 91% of homeowners won't even consider a shop rated under 4 stars (BrightLocal 2026), so rating and volume both matter. Start here: how to get your first 50 reviews.

body.answer: You rank near where you're based, not everywhere you drive.
body.html: Contractors routinely set a 60-mile service radius and wonder why they rank nowhere. Proximity to the searcher is a real factor — a huge radius doesn't buy you reach, it just dilutes you. Set the areas you actually work, and build separate proof (reviews mentioning the town, job photos, a page per city) for the places you want to win.

body.h2: 4. Your name, address, and phone don't match everywhere
body.answer: Inconsistent NAP data makes you look like two businesses.
body.html: If your shop is "Smith Heating & Air" on Google, "Smith HVAC" on Facebook, and an old cell number on three directories, Google has to guess which listing is real. Pick one exact name/address/phone and make every listing match it, character for character. This is boring and it works.

body.h2: 5. You're suspended — and nobody emailed you
body.answer: Suspended listings vanish with no warning.
body.html: Suspensions happen over things like a virtual office address, keyword stuffing in the business name, or a category change. Sign in to your profile and look for a suspension notice. If you're suspended, no amount of posting fixes it — you appeal first, then rebuild.

body.h2: Then: don't waste the ranking you earn
body.answer: Ranking sends the call. Answering it books the job.
body.html: Showing up is only half of it. 78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first (Lead Connect 2026), replying in 5 minutes rather than 30 makes you up to 100x more likely to connect (MIT Sloan 2026), and the average shop still misses 14% of its calls (CallRail 2026). Getting into the map pack and then missing the phone is the most expensive mistake in this whole list.

faq.q: Why is my business not showing up on Google Maps?
faq.a: Usually one of five things: an incomplete Google Business Profile, too few reviews to compete (median ~519 for HVAC, ~337 for plumbers), a service area set too wide, inconsistent name/address/phone across listings, or a suspension you weren't notified about. Work them in that order.

faq.q: How long does it take to rank in the Google map pack?
faq.a: Months, not days — and it tracks your review growth more than anything else. 91% of homeowners won't consider a shop under 4 stars (BrightLocal 2026), so build rating and volume steadily rather than chasing a shortcut.

faq.q: Does a bigger service area help me rank in more towns?
faq.a: No. Proximity matters, so an oversized radius dilutes you instead of extending you. Set the areas you actually serve and build real proof — reviews, photos, a page per city — for the towns you want to win.
